title: Flipped classroom learning in K-12 redox chemistry: learning gains, video engagement, and implementation factors
content: Flipped classroom instruction shifts initial engagement with new content outside the classroom, often through explanatory videos, and uses classroom time for application-oriented activities. This study critically examines the assumption that flipped classroom inherently leads to superior learning outcomes compared to traditional instruction, particularly in K-12 redox chemistry. As one of the largest single empirical studies to date on flipped classroom in K-12 chemistry (N = 349) and employing a more rigorous methodological approach than many previous studies, it provides robust insights into its effectiveness and influencing factors. Using a quasi-experimental design, we investigated students from sixteen K-12 classes. The analyses did not detect statistically significant differences in redox learning gains between flipped classroom and traditional instruction. However, subgroup analyses suggest that repeated exposure to instructional explanations, both during pre-class video preparation and in-class instruction, plays a crucial role in learning success. Beyond learning outcomes, additional analyses identified factors associated with learning gains in flipped and non-flipped chemistry classrooms, including class size, teachers’ years of service, and students’ engagement with instructional videos. Log data provided insight into students’ engagement patterns, showing that students in the flipped classroom group accessed the videos more frequently and watched them for longer than students in the traditional teaching group. This study contributes to the existing literature by making students’ actual engagement with video-based learning opportunities visible and showing that flipped classroom instruction in redox chemistry should be understood as conditional rather than automatically superior to traditional teaching.
